correctness.rationale: Exact normalized positive-integer laws and strictly convex exponent imply monotone opposing hazards. The unique Lambert threshold decides the first sign, hence the complete hazard order. Survival-ratio factors have one direction change and their ratio tends to zero, yielding the unique survival-order reversal. As alpha grows, omega at the moving crossing converges to the unique root of a monotone scalar equation; the exponential-over-linear R asymptotic proves the log(alpha)+loglog(alpha) formula. A summable infinite-product correction proves the geometric tail equivalent and exact exponential moment-domain; a finite standard-library checker independently stress-tests identities.

broader_coverage.reasoning: Universal hazard-product constructions and geometric-limit criteria are older general techniques; the comparison requires their application to two distinct sequences determined by the same nonpolynomial omega. The generalized-Rayleigh distribution has a different survival generator and cannot imply this exact threshold or scaling. A general statement about geometric tails does not determine the positive asymptotic constant, exact MGF boundary, and one-change survival order for this model.

It does not state a comparison between the survival model's true failure hazard and that decreasing hazard, their unique intersection and consequent single survival crossing. Extracting their alpha-dependent intersection, its two-term large-alpha location, and the parameter-independent MGF threshold requires the additional convexity, ratio, singular-root asymptotics, and infinite-product proof supplied here.

value.rationale: The paired discretizations are an established reliability-model choice, and their common generating survival does not reveal whether one uniformly dominates the other. The exact alpha*(theta) separates global stochastic ordering from a unique reversal; the log(alpha)+loglog(alpha) location quantifies delayed detection, and the exact, parameter-independent exponential-moment domain quantifies a radical change of tail risk. This is a complete, naturally motivated comparison rather than a small isolated formula or a pure normalization check.
